## Cognitive Models in Plain `brms`

[`brms`](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/) can fit some cognitive models on its
own. `wiener()` is the classic four-parameter drift diffusion model,
`shifted_lognormal()` a shifted reaction-time distribution, and
`exgaussian()` the ex-Gaussian. They are among the most widely used and best
tested families in the field, they need no extra package, and if one of them
is the model you need and your data have been trimmed of anticipatory
responses, plain `brms` is the simplest option. 

But it comes with limitations:

- **A short list of models.** No race models (LBA, RDM, LNR), no between-trial
  variability in the DDM, and no shifted distributions beyond the LogNormal.
- **Non-standard parametrisations.** In `exgaussian()`, `mu` is
  the mean of the whole distribution, not of its Gaussian component as in the
  experimental-psychology literature, which is confusing (see [Geller, Angele & Makowski, 2026](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/kdcxa_v2)).
- **Nothing for fast responses.** Very fast responses (below `ndt`) are not 
  allowed, and will make the fitting fail, which requires extra preprocessing 
  (trimming the fast responses) and fidly parametrization.
- **Flat priors and random starts.** Several parameters are left with flat
  priors, and chains start at random values that, leading to a lot of initialization
  failures.

This is why bespoke packages exist. They add models and make them convenient to use.

## `cogmod`'s Design Principles

![](https://media1.tenor.com/m/rkI1a8s2Z6QAAAAd/todd-howard-it-just-works.gif){style="float: right; width: 160px; margin: 0 0 0.5em 1.5em;" fig-alt="It just works"}

`cogmod`'s aim is to bring cognitive
models within the familiar realm of regular `brms` models, so that the
standard Bayesian workflow (fit, check, compare, summarise, report, predict, etc.) "just works"
on them. A `cogmod` model *is* a `brm()` call. The family goes in `bf()` like
any `brms` family, and the only extra bit is the need for a `cogmod_stanvars()`,
which adds the necessary Stan functions.

### Transparency

Nothing sits between you and the model. `brms::stancode(f, data = df, stanvars = cogmod_stanvars(f))` prints the whole program, family functions included, and that program is the one that gets compiled. Priors and starting
values are not applied behind the scenes: `cogmod_priors()` and
`cogmod_inits()` return ordinary `brms` objects that you pass to `brm()`
yourself, so they are written into every script, and can be printed, inspected,
overwritten and edited there. The source code carries the reasoning for every prior, link
and constant.

### Lightness

`cogmod` is a set of families, not a layer. It defines no class for fitted
models and no methods for `brmsfit`. Random-effect structures, smooths,
within-chain threading, `update()` and, on the RT-only families, `cens()` work
just as for any other `brms` models.

Inside the package, each family is defined once. A single registry entry
generates its Stan code, its R density and random generator, its `log_lik()`,
`posterior_predict()` and `posterior_epred()` methods, its parameter checks
and its priors, so the R and Stan sides cannot drift apart. The densities are
exported (`dcogmod_*()`, `rcogmod_*()` and, for most families, `pcogmod_*()`),
so a model can be simulated or used in a parameter-recovery study without
fitting anything.

### A Minimal, Consistent API

`cogmod`'s interface has essentially four functions. The family and
`cogmod_stanvars()` are required. `cogmod_priors()` and `cogmod_inits()` are
optional. The pattern is the same for every family.

### brms' Quirks Are Inherited Too

Some of `brms`'s conventions and idiosyncrasies apply. Parameters are named the
way `brms` names them: `mu` for the main parameters, even if they are drift rates, 
as in `brms`'s own `wiener()`. A parameter written in `bf()` lives on its link scale, while one left out is
estimated on its natural scale. The best way to learn how to use `cogmod` is to learn how to use `brms`, 
which is the point of the package.

### Post-Processing by the Packages That Do It Best

`cogmod` has no `summary()`, plotting, marginal-effects or reporting functions
of its own. It implements what `brms` asks of a family, and everything downstream
builds on those: `loo`, `pp_check()` and `bayesplot`, and the packages built
for `brms` models, such as easystats (`parameters`, `modelbased`,
`performance`, `bayestestR`, `report`), `marginaleffects` and `emmeans`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false

parameters::parameters(m)

# Non-decision time by condition, and its difference between conditions
marginaleffects::avg_predictions(m, by = "Condition", dpar = "ndt")
marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(m, variables = "Condition", dpar = "ndt")

loo::loo_compare(loo(m_brms), loo(m))
```

These packages are maintained by people who specialise in them and are used
on every kind of `brms` model, so a `cogmod` fit benefits from each of their
improvements without a line of `cogmod` changing. Being also the coauthor of **easystats**, 
I (Dominique Makowski) made sure that its awesome post-processing features
also work seamlessly for `cogmod` models.

### Speed, Measured

The giam of `cogmod` is to fit these models correctly *and* as fast as
they can be fitted, and neither is assumed:

- **Gradients are checked, not only values.** An R density and a Stan density
  can agree on every value while the gradient the sampler follows is wrong.
  On every pull request, a continuous-integration job compares each family's
  gradient with finite differences over a grid that includes responses in the
  far tails.
- **Every change to a Stan density is timed** against the version it replaces,
  and a slower gradient is treated as a regression and investigated.
- **Features and documentation is there to help speed.** `cogmod_inits()` starts chains in a sensible
  region, and `cogmod_warmstart()` reuses the adaptation of one fit for the
  next. The [Performance](performance.html) article covers the rest.


## Alternatives

### `bmm`

[`bmm`](https://popov-lab.github.io/bmm/) ([Frischkorn & Popov,
2025](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-025-02643-0)) is a great atlernative, also built on `brms`,
and differs from `cogmod` in design rather than in quality. It puts an
interface between the user and `brms`. A model is written with its own formula
function, `bmf()`, using the parameter names of the model's literature, with
the response variables named in the model constructor. `bmm()` translates this
into a `brms` formula, family and Stan code, checks the data (reaction times
in milliseconds, responses not coded 0/1), applies model-specific priors and
starting values, calls `brm()`, and returns a `bmmfit`
with methods of its own: a `summary()`, a `conditional_effects()` that shows
parameters on their native scale, a `pp_check()` that can check every
observable of the likelihood. Contamination is handled
before the fit, with `flag_contaminant_rts()` identifying fast guesses and
attention lapses for you to remove.

That is a full solution from beginning to end, in one vocabulary. It suits
users who are new to these models and want one package to take them from data
to a reported fit, without necessarily wanting cognitive models to sit
alongside their other `brms` models in the same workflow. The costs are the
mirror of `cogmod`'s choices: a layer and a set of methods that have to keep
pace with `brms`, and conveniences that stay within the package.


### Outside `brms`

[EMC2](https://cran.r-project.org/package=EMC2) fits hierarchical DDM, LBA,
RDM and LNR models with particle-based samplers in R, using its own design
language and post-processing. [HSSM](https://github.com/lnccbrown/HSSM)
(Python) adds likelihood approximation networks for models without a
closed-form likelihood. [`rtdists`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rtdists)
provides densities and random generation for the DDM and LBA, without
fitting.

## Choosing

- **Plain `brms`** if its native families cover your model (shifted LogNormal,
  ex-Gaussian with its overall-mean parametrisation, four-parameter DDM) and
  your data have been trimmed of anticipatory responses.
- **`bmm`** for visual working memory, M3, EZ-diffusion from summary
  statistics, or if you prefer an integrated
  toolkit with a model-specific vocabulary.
- **`cogmod`** for race models, the DDM with between-trial variability, a
  choice of RT distributions to compare, rating-scale models, or outliers
  modelled inside the likelihood, and whenever you want the model to remain a
  plain `brms` call.
